newsitem.title: FRANCE: LVMH boosts Grand Met stake in puzzling gambit.
newsitem.headline: LVMH boosts Grand Met stake in puzzling gambit.

text.p: France's LVMH raised its stake in Britain's Grand Metropolitan to more than six percent on Thursday as part of a two-pronged attack to foil the planned Grand Met-Guinness merger, industry sources said.
Grand Met confirmed that LVMH (Louis Vuitton Moet Hennessy) had increased its stake to 6.29 percent from 3.2 percent after buying 125 million shares for 787.5 million pounds.
LVMH declined to comment, but the luxury goods company said earlier in the week when it first bought Grand Met shares that it had no intention of launching a takeover bid.

An industry source said LVMH was preparing to buy as much as 10 percent of Grand Met to put pressure on the British group to drop the merger plan, which faces possible U.S. and European antitrust objections, and consider LVMH's alternative proposal.

LVMH Chairman Bernard Arnault wants to create a group combining LVMH's Moet & Chandon and Hennessy brands with Guinness's Johnny Walker, Dewars and Gordon's Gin labels and, possibly, Grand Met's Smirnoff, J&B and Baileys brands.
Just how Arnault proposes to achieve that objective was not clear, but he has not lost many fights in his career.

LVMH, Guinness's largest shareholder with 14 percent, had already set out to wreck the Grand Met-Guinness merger plan by trying to buy Guinness out of their valuable joint distribution ventures, which own the rights to market Guinness brands in France, the United States and much of the Far East for 10 years.

LVMH requested arbitration from the International Chamber of Commerce last week to uphold its right to exercise those options, shredding the new Grand Met-Guinness (GMG) group's distribution network, if the companies go ahead and merge.
Guinness says LVMH has no right to exercise the options, and both sides confidently say they have legal experts' backing.
An industry source said LVMH took the Grand Met stake because the arbitration could take months.
"(Arbitration) wouldn't block the merger anyway," the source said. "LVMH felt they might be more persuasive if they took a stake in Grand Met. That would oblige Grand Met to listen."

Most analysts were unclear as to LVMH's strategy. To block the merger outright, it would need more than 25 percent of Grand Met alone or with an ally. Analysts did not see Arnault spending 30 billion francs to buy that big a stake.

LVMH's share price has fallen since Arnault began making inroads into Grand Met. "People don't like that cavalier attitude. If he's going to pursue them with legal means, fine, but now he's buying stock," a Paris broker said.
"Investors must be saying, what are you doing? That's our money. And if you scuttle the deal, Grand Met will only go down in price," said analyst John Wakely at Lehman Brothers.

One analyst said Arnault may want to prove he is a force to be reckoned with. "He's going to be a thorn in GMG's side until he gets what he wants, or at least until he gets something more than what he's being offered, which is nothing."
Arnault was not expected to be invited to join GMG's board as his 14 percent Guinness stake gives him seven percent of GMG.
Another analyst said Arnault may not feel confident of victory and may be trying to ensure for accounting purposes that he has a sufficient holding to consolidate the income.

Cecile d'Estais at Paribas Capital Markets said he may be trying to secure at least 30 percent of the combined drinks operations of the three companies in the event that he succeeds in pushing the creation of such a group.

She said he could do that only by buying Grand Met shares, as he was barred from making unsolicited purchases of Guinness stock. A few months ago, LVMH sold a seven percent stake in Guinness to help pay for its $2.6 billion acquisition of a controlling stake in Duty Free Shoppers.
